title: Request for Rehearing of the Michigan Attorney General re the 03/19/2026 Order under EL26-36.

documents.name: EL26-36-001 - FERC_Request for Rehearing_4.20.2026.pdf
documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                  BEFORE THE
                    FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                            )
Northern Indiana Public Service Company LLC )
                                            )
       v.                                   )                            Docket No. EL26-36-001
                                            )
Midcontinent Independent System             )
   Operator, Inc.                           )
                                            )

                             REQUEST FOR REHEARING OF
                          THE MICHIGAN ATTORNEY GENERAL

         Pursuant to Section 313(a) of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”), 16 U.S.C. § 825l (2024),
cand Rule 713 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy Regulatory
Commission (“Commission”), 1 Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel, on behalf of the people
of the State of Michigan, requests rehearing of the Order issued on March 19, 2026, granting the
complaint (the Complaint) filed by Northern Indiana Public Service Company (“NIPSCO” or “the
Company”) requesting the Commission require adoption of a cost recovery mechanism for costs
to comply with the Department of Energy Order 2 issued pursuant to Section 202(c) of Federal
Power Act (FPA) to prevent the scheduled retirement of NIPSCO’s R.M. Schahfer Generating
Station Units 17 and 18 (the “Schahfer Units”).

I.       Concise Statement of Issues and Specifications of Error
     •   The Commission abused its discretion by granting the Complaint before the legal validity
         of the DOE Order has been adjudicated. The Commission arbitrarily and capriciously
         failed to respond meaningfully to objections raised in the docket and engage with the
         evidence before it. Am. Gas Ass’n v. FERC, 593 F.3d 14, 19 (D.C. Cir. 2010); Laclede Gas
         Co. v. FERC, 873 F.2d 1494, 1498, 277 U.S. App. D.C. 237 (D.C. Cir. 1989).
     •   The Commission acted contrary to law by granting the Complaint on the basis of the ultra
         vires DOE Order. See, e.g., Michigan v. E.P.A., 268 F.3d 1075, 1081 (D.C. Cir. (2001).


1
         18 C.F.R. § 385.713.
2
         Department of Energy Order No. 202-25-12 (December 23, 2025) (the “DOE Order”).


                                                  1
       •   The Commission acted contrary to law by granting the Complaint before holding a hearing
          as required under 16 U.S.C. § 824a(c)(1). See, e.g., Nat. Res. Def. Council v. Reilly, 983
          F.2d 259, 261 (D.C. Cir. 1993); see also, e.g., Nat’l Auto. Dealers Ass’n v. Fed Trade
          Comm’n, 127 F.4th 549, 559 (5th Cir. 2025).
      •   The Commission erred in accepting the proposed cost allocation to MISO Local Resource
          Zones 1-7. The Commission’s determination that the DOE Order establishes that its
          beneficiaries are LSEs in Local Zones 1-7 is arbitrary and capricious because it is
          inconsistent with Commission precedent, is not supported by substantial evidence in the
          record, and fails to respond meaningfully to objections raised in the docket. New York
          Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc. Niagara Mohawk Power Corp., 184 FERC ¶ 61,059 at P 47
          (2023); Consol. Edison Co. of New York, Inc. et al., 180 FERC ¶ 61,106, 61,739 at P 50
          (2022); New England Power Generators Ass’n v. FERC, 881 F.3d 202, 210, 434 U.S. App.
          D.C. 225 (D.C. Cir. 2018); Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co.,
          463 U.S. 29, 43, 103 S. Ct. 2856, 77 L. Ed. 2d 443 (1983).

II.       Request for Rehearing
                 a. The Commission abused its discretion by granting the Complaint before
                    the legal validity of the DOE Order has been adjudicated.
          The Commission’s determination to grant the Complaint while the validity of the DOE
Order remains contested and is being adjudicated before the federal courts is an abuse of its
discretion. The Commission failed to evaluate the potential for deferred action on the cost recovery
mechanism, nor did it engage meaningfully with arguments before it that there is good cause for
deferring action on the Complaint until the legal validity of the DOE Order is resolved.
          Under the APA’s abuse of discretion standard, “an action by the Commission may be set
aside ‘if the agency has relied on factors which Congress has not intended it to consider, entirely
failed to consider an important aspect of the problem, offered an explanation for its decision that
runs counter to the evidence before the agency, or is so implausible that it could not be ascribed to
a difference in view or the product of agency expertise.’” Env’t Def. Fund v. FERC, 2 F4th 953,
967 (D.C. Cir. 2021) (quoting Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Ass’n of the United States, Inc. v. State
Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 29, 43, 103 S. Ct. 2856, 2866 (1983)); see also Burlington
Truck Lines, Inc. v. United States, 371 U.S. 156, 167 (1962).




                                                  2
          The Commission has discretion as to whether and how to resolve questions of cost recovery
concerning 202(c) orders. 3 Section 202(c) further presents no temporal requirement for how
quickly the Commission must resolve such questions. 4 The Michigan Attorney General raised this
issue in her Protest, requesting, that “[i]f the Commission is not inclined to deny the complaint on
its merits, it should use the discretion afforded by FPA Section 202(c)—which makes clear that
issuing an order to prescribe compensation or reimbursement is discretionary, not mandatory, and
sets no timeline in which such matters must be resolved—to deny the complaint without prejudice
as prematurely filed.” 5
         The timing of the Commission’s Order is significant given the potential implications of
prematurely initiating a cost recovery mechanism. On the one hand, there is no harm to NIPSCO
if the cost recovery process is delayed until an adjudication is made on the validity of the DOE
Order, which is currently the subject of review on appeal. 6 On the other hand, invalidity of the
DOE Order would mean that cost recovery under Commission’s Order would be unjust and
unreasonable and would constitute a violation of the filed-rate doctrine. 7 NIPSCO has filed its
complaint precisely because the MISO tariff does not permit cost recovery for the costs it has
incurred to make the Schahfer Units available to operate. If the DOE Order is struck down by the
courts, the Commission would have no choice but to refund any charges to MISO’s customers
because even “the Commission itself has no power to alter a rate retroactively.” 8 There is thus a
significant risk to MISO customers if costs are improperly collected, and a risk of administrative


3
       See U.S.C. § 824a(c)(1) (the Commission “may prescribe by supplemental order such
terms as it finds to be just and reasonable, including the compensation or reimbursement which
should be paid to or by any such party.”) (emphasis added).
4
         Id.
5
         See the Attorney General’s Protest at 4.
6
         People of Mich. v U.S. Dep’t of Energy, appeal docketed, No. 26-1077 (D.C. Cir. April 2,
2026).
7
        Old Dominion Elec. Coop. v. FERC, 892 F.3d 1223, 1226 (D.C. Cir. 2018) (“The Act also
empowers the Commission to fix or change rates and charges, but only prospectively. 16 U.S.C.
§ 824e(a). When a utility wishes to alter the rates it charges, it must provide sixty-days’ notice to
the Commission and file new rate schedules “stating plainly the change or changes to be made in
the schedule or schedules then in force and the time when the change or changes will go into
effect.” Id. § 824d(d).”).
8
         Arkansas Louisiana Gas Co. v. Hall, 453 U.S. 571, 578 (1981).


                                                    3
 costs in attempting a post-hoc unwinding of that cost recovery if the DOE Order is found to be
invalid.
       The Commission could have avoided these problems by simply waiting to issue an Order
as it has discretion to do under the FPA. While the Commission’s Order appears to acknowledge
the Attorney General’s prematurity argument, 9 it presents only a conclusory finding on that issue
that “[w]e also reject commenters’ request to delay action on the Proposed Tariff Provision until
the rehearing proceeding at DOE is resolved, as prompt action on the Complaint can help to
mitigate potential regulatory uncertainty.” 10 No other support or explanation is provided. “In cases
where parties raise reasonable alternatives to the Commission’s position . . . reasoned
decisionmaking requires considering those alternatives.” Am. Gas Ass’n v. FERC, 593 F.3d 14, 19,
389 U.S. App. D.C. 162 (D.C. Cir. 2010). “Where a party raises facially reasonable alternatives
to FERC’s decision . . . the agency must either consider those alternatives or give some reason,
within its broad discretion . . . for declining to do so.” Id., quoting Laclede Gas Co. v. FERC, 873
F.2d 1494, 1498, 277 U.S. App. D.C. 237 (D.C. Cir. 1989) (emphasis in original).
       The Commission’s statement that “prompt action… can help to mitigate potential
regulatory uncertainty” fails to present sufficient support, reasoning, or consideration of the
Attorney General’s positions, such as per the caselaw identified above. For one, the Commission
presents no reasoning as to why its refusal to defer a decision would better serve to mitigate
regulatory uncertainty. See, e.g., Am. Gas Ass’n v. FERC, 593 F.3d 14, 19, 389 U.S. App. D.C. 162
(D.C. Cir. 2010). It’s conclusory finding likewise fails to acknowledge, let alone evaluate in
comparison, the Attorney General’s observations in her protest as to why delaying a determination
in this matter would be preferable, including that a delayed determination would be better to
“safeguard against the potential imposition of unjust and unreasonable charges, and to avoid
administrative inefficiency that would result if the DOE Order changes in scope or is invalidated,
necessitating refunds.” 11


9
        See Commission Order at P 18 (“Alternatively, the Michigan Attorney General requests
that the Commission, under the discretion afforded the Commission under FPA section 202(c),
issue an order deferring any finding, on the basis that the Proposed Tariff Provision is premature
until the rehearing requests at DOE are resolved.”).
10
       Id. at P 39.
11
       Attorney General’s Protest at 4 – 5.


                                                 4
        Further, the Commission’s references to its orders in the Consumers Energy matter 12 only
undermine its conclusion on this topic. While litigation of the underlying 202(c) order in that
matter is advancing, the Commission’s decision to grant Consumers Energy’s complaint has only
served to drive additional litigation in the interim; its decision has not served to mitigate regulatory
uncertainty. For example, Consumers Energy has noted that it is seeking recovery of legal and
consulting costs for its participation in its FERC cost-recovery proceeding. 13 Such expenses will
have been categorically unnecessary should the underlying 202(c) order be invalidated. The
Commission’s Order here makes no attempt to reckon with the consequences of its decision in that
case or otherwise assess how deferral of its decision on the present complaint would serve to avoid
inefficiencies. By failing to meaningfully engage with this question, and failing to articulate any
basis for its decision on the same, the Commission has abused its discretion under Section 202(c).
See, e.g., Env’t Def. Fund v. FERC, 2 F4th 953, 967 (D.C. Cir. 2021).

               b. The Commission acted contrary to law by granting the Complaint on the
                  basis of an ultra vires Order.

       Absent a legally valid 202(c) order, the Commission is not authorized to grant a cost
recovery mechanism under that statute; the “compensation and reimbursement” provisions of
U.S.C. § 824a(c)(1) are conditioned on the existence of an order to be implemented. The Michigan
Attorney General has submitted lengthy argument in this matter and pending in the D.C. Circuit
Court of Appeals as to why the DOE Order is itself invalid. Absent statutory authorization, an
agency’s “action is plainly contrary to law and cannot stand.” Michigan v. E.P.A., 268 F.3d 1075,
1081 (D.C. Cir. 2001).
       The entirety of the present matter is premised on the legal force of the DOE Order; 14 the
Commission’s Order presents no other legal basis for granting NIPSCO’s Complaint. Thus, as the
underlying DOE Order is invalid, there is no legal basis for Commission action here. Likewise,

12
       194 FERC ¶ 61,215 at P 39, FN 75 (citing to Consumers v. MISO, 192 FERC ¶ 61,158 at
P 41; Rehearing Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,228 at P 43).
13
        See, Consumers Energy’s revised application in FERC docket ER26-1138-001 (filed
February 13, 2026), Exhibit A at 13 (“For example, the costs of preparing this filing and
participating in this proceeding are Order Costs associated with the May 2025 DOE Order.”).
14
       The Commission’s authority pursuant to either 16 U.S.C. § 824a(c)(1) or 10 C.F.R. §
205.376 is premised on the existence of a valid 202(C) order, and the Commission does not
dispute that point in its Order.


                                                   5
 as raised in the Michigan Attorney General’s Protest, cost recovery under that illegal order is
contrary to law as unjust and unreasonable as well as a violation of the filed-rate doctrine.

               c. The Commission acted contrary to law by granting the Complaint before
                  holding a hearing as required under 16 U.S.C. § 824a(c)(1).
       Under 16 U.S.C. § 824a(c)(1) the Commission may issue a supplemental order “after
hearing held either before or after such order takes effect….” Pursuant to the Commission’s rules
of procedure, the term “hearing” presents a specific meaning and entails specific requirements.
For example, per rule 502 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice, 18 C.F.R. § 385.502, Orders or
Notices of hearings by FERC must include specific details, such as the “presiding officer” and “the
date, time, and location of the hearing or prehearing conference, if known.” Section 385 of the
Commission’s Rules further describes the required procedures for hearings, such as the right of
participants to present evidence as part of hearings. 15 The Commission here has neither noticed
nor held a hearing as described under its rules of procedure.
       An agency’s failure to abide by unambiguous statutory duties or procedures constitutes a
violation of the APA. See, e.g., Nat. Res. Def. Council v. Reilly, 983 F.2d 259, 261 (D.C. Cir. 1993)
(finding an APA violation where the EPA failed to promulgate certain standards as required by the
plain language of the Clean Air Act: “because the language of section 202(a)(6) plainly imposes a
mandatory duty, we agree that EPA's decision not to promulgate ORVR standards was beyond the
pale of its statutory authority”); see also, e.g., Nat’l Auto. Dealers Ass’n v. Fed Trade Comm’n,
127 F.4th 549, 559 (5th Cir. 2025) (finding an APA violation where the FTC failed to conduct
statutorily-required advance notice of proposed rulemaking).
       Here, FPA Section 202(c) requires in its plain language that any supplemental order by
FERC can occur only “after hearing held.” 16 U.S.C. § 824a(c)(1). The Commission’s failure to
abide by this requirement thus constitutes a violation of the APA under the standards set forth in
the caselaw cited above and elsewhere. And through the Commission’s failure to conduct a hearing
in this matter, the Michigan Attorney General has been prejudiced by a missed opportunity to
further develop and present evidence for the Commission’s consideration in forming a decision on
this nuanced matter.




15
       18 C.F.R § 385.505.


                                                 6
                 d. The Commission erred in accepting the proposed cost allocation to MISO
                   Local Resource Zones 1-7.
        The Commission further acted in an arbitrary and capricious manner by ordering that the
proposed cost allocation be limited to only MISO Zones 1-7. As set forth in the Michigan Attorney
General’s Protest, the DOE Order purports to address a MISO-wide emergency. 16 It does not limit
its assessment of the emergency to particular zones in MISO.
        The Commission’s determination that the scope of the “benefit” of the Order is best
determined by looking at the scope of the purported “emergency” as described by the DOE Order
is inconsistent with Commission precedent. Assuming arguendo the validity of the DOE Order,
then the operation of the Schahfer Units would be necessary to comply with a federal law.
Accordingly, any “benefit” of its operation would accrue broadly throughout the region. Under
Commission precedent, cost allocation is roughly commensurate with the benefits where the costs
to comply with a law are shared among customers across the law’s applicable jurisdiction. For
example, where New York State law required investment in certain transmission infrastructure to
achieve State policy objectives, the Commission held that it is consistent with cost causation
principles to allocate the costs of those projects on a volumetric load-ratio share basis across New
York State. 17 The Commission acted arbitrarily and capriciously by failing to address or explain
its divergence from this relevant precedent. 18
        The reasoning from Niagara Mohawk Power Corp is particularly salient here since there
is no objective benefit to Miso Zones 1-7 from the continued operation of the Schahfer Units. As
identified in the Michigan Attorney General’s Protest, NIPSCO and MISO had already accounted
for the retirement of the Schahfer Units in capacity planning through IRP and Attachment Y
processes. 19

16
       See the Michigan Attorney General’s Protest at pages 8 – 9 (“c. To be consistent with
cost-causation principles, cost allocation must be RTO-wide”).
17
        New York Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc. Niagara Mohawk Power Corp., 184 FERC ¶ 61,059
at P 47 (2023); Consol. Edison Co. of New York, Inc. et al., 180 FERC ¶ 61,106, 61,739 at P 50
(2022).
18
       Belmont Mun. Light Dep't v. FERC, 38 F.4th 173, 184–85 (D.C. Cir. 2022) (“[I]t is
textbook administrative law that an agency must provide a reasoned explanation for departing
from precedent or treating similar situations differently”) (internal citation and quotation
omitted).
19
        Attorney General’s Protest at 2 – 3.


                                                  7
        In granting the Complaint on this point, the Commission’s Order cites only “the DOE
Order’s reliance on statements in MISO’s presentation on the Planning Resource Auction Results
for Planning Year 2025-2026 that ‘new capacity additions were insufficient to offset the negative
impacts of decreased accreditation, suspension/retirements and external resources.’” 20 But as
discussed in the Michigan Attorney General’s Protest, the PRA slide in question is not discussing
results from only the MISO North and Central zones, it is discussing the results for the whole
PRA. 21 In contrast, at Slide 4, which considers the PRA results for the North/Central and South
zones separately, MISO notes that the North/Central zones have a higher effective summer margin
at 10.1% compared to the South zones at 8.7%. 22 To the extent that the DOE Order could establish
that an emergency exists at all (which it cannot), that emergency would extend across the MISO
region, and would not be limited to any particular MISO zones. The Commission has erred by
relying on the DOE Order’s false characterization of the PRA results as pertaining to Zones 1-7.
Given that the limited facts cited by the DOE Order as the basis for its purported “emergency” are
overwhelmingly facts that apply to the MISO region as a whole, 23 the Commission’s determination
that “the most reasonable reading” of the DOE Order is that an emergency exists within MISO
North and Central is arbitrary and capricious. 24
       The Administrative Procedure Act’s arbitrary-and-capricious standard “requires the agency
to ‘examine the relevant data and articulate a satisfactory explanation for its action including a
rational connection between the facts found and the choice made.’” New England Power
Generators Ass’n v. FERC, 881 F.3d 202, 210, 434 U.S. App. D.C. 225 (D.C. Cir. 2018) (quoting


20
       See Commission Order at P 37.
21
       See Michigan Attorney General’s Protest at 8.
22
       Id.
23
       DOE Order at 1-4.
24
        PPL Wallingford Energy LLC v. FERC, 419 F.3d 1194, 1198 (D.C. Cir. 2005) (“An
agency’s failure to respond meaningfully to objections raised by a party renders its decision
arbitrary and capricious . . . . unless the agency answers objections that on their face seem
legitimate, its decision can hardly be classified as reasoned.”); Env’t Def. Fund v. FERC, 2 F.4th
953, 967–68 (D.C. Cir. 2021) (“A passing reference to relevant factors ... is not sufficient to
satisfy the Commission’s obligation to carry out ‘reasoned’ and ‘principled’ decisionmaking”)
(citation omitted); Black Oak Energy, LLC v. FERC, 725 F.3d 230, 244 (D.C. Cir. 2013)
(“Because FERC failed to explain how it analyzed this crucial aspect of the case, we hold that
the Commission acted arbitrarily and capriciously.”).


                                                    8
 Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 29, 43, 103 S. Ct. 2856, 77
L. Ed. 2d 443 (1983). The Commission arbitrarily and capriciously failed to engage with the
evidence presented by the Michigan Attorney General or adequately explain how its finding can
be reconciled with that contrary evidence in the record.


III.   CONCLUSION
       For the foregoing reasons, the Michigan Attorney General’s Request for Rehearing
should be granted.
